title: Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan
hook: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree

segments.voice: Yesterday: kirtan. A scholar set down his arguments and took God's names into the street.

Step on a blade of grass and it bends flat. Lift your foot and, after a moment, it stands back up. No complaint, no grudge. A tree stands in the sun all day and gives its shade to whoever sits down, even the one with the axe. Those two humble things, grass and a tree, open a short verse that Chaitanya's tradition treasures. On the last day with the saints of bhakti, it answers a practical question: how do you keep singing?
screen: `GRASS BENDS, THEN STANDS.` → `A TREE GIVES ITS SHADE.` → `HOW DO YOU KEEP SINGING?`

segments.voice: Chaitanya's followers keep a short set of verses under his name, called the Shikshashtakam, his teaching. One goes, in plain English: be humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree. Give honor to others, and ask none for yourself. Then you can sing the name of Hari always. Read it as the fine print under kirtan. Anyone can join the song on the first try. Staying in it is harder. Pride wants the lead line. Impatience wants the song to end. Wanting respect turns a chorus into a competition. The verse clears all three away, and what's left can keep singing. His tradition remembers him living it out in Puri, on the coast, where he spent his later years near the temple of Jagannath. At the great chariot festival, the Ratha Yatra, he's remembered dancing before the rolling chariot with groups of kirtan singers, lost in the names, the whole crowd caught up with him. Now look back over these four weeks. Andal and Nammalvar, singing to Vishnu in Tamil. The Nayanars, singing to Shiva. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram, walking and singing in Maharashtra. Kabir and his sharp couplets. Tulsidas and Hanuman's song. Surdas in Yashoda's yard. Mira, laughing over the cup. And Chaitanya in the street with a drum. Different languages, different names for God. One habit: they sang to God as if God were near.
screen: `HUMBLER THAN GRASS.` · `MORE PATIENT THAN A TREE.` · `DANCING BEFORE THE CHARIOT.` · then, large: `THEY SANG AS IF GOD WERE NEAR.`

segments.voice: Feel where your body meets the floor, and for a few breaths be like grass: low, rooted, flexible, letting go of one small need to be right or to be noticed. Then be like the tree, standing in the sun so others can rest in your shade, and bring to mind one person you could honor without needing anything back. If you pray, let a name of God ride gently on the breath.
Shikshashtakam. Chaitanya's short teaching verses, the fine print that keeps the song going: humbler than grass, more patient than a tree.
Your line: humbler than grass. Next come the modern teachers, starting with a temple priest near Calcutta. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas recite the Shikshashtakam, and the grass-and-tree verse is often sung or quoted before kirtan; at Puri's Ratha Yatra, kirtan groups sing and dance before Jagannath's chariot.

chat.says: Doesn't humbler than grass just mean letting everyone walk all over you?
options: It means dropping pride and the need for honor, so you can keep singing God's name.
Yes, it means agreeing with anyone who argues with you, to keep the peace.

chat.meaning: The verse asks for humility, patience and honoring others without asking honor back. Then, it says, you can sing Hari's name always.

Shikshashtakam.meaning: eight verses of teaching kept under Chaitanya's name

Hari.meaning: a name of Vishnu, and so of Krishna

Puri.meaning: a temple town on the coast, home of Jagannath

Jagannath.meaning: lord of the world, the form of Krishna worshiped at Puri

Ratha Yatra.meaning: the chariot festival of Jagannath at Puri

Chaitanya.meaning: the Bengali saint remembered for bringing kirtan into the streets
